originalGroup.material:
A. Choosing a club and taking a journey

A school may offer more clubs than you can reasonably join. Choosing well does not mean finding the one with the most impressive name. It means understanding what you want to try and what regular participation would involve.

Read the description beyond its first line. A photography club might spend as much time discussing pictures as taking them. ____1____ Knowing the ordinary activities helps prevent disappointment based on an imagined version of the club.

Attend a trial session if one is available. Notice how beginners are welcomed and whether questions receive useful answers. ____2____ A single enjoyable demonstration does not necessarily show what a normal meeting feels like.

Check the practical commitment. A club that meets after the last bus may be difficult to attend even if its subject interests you. ____3____ Enthusiasm is more likely to last when the arrangement fits your week.

Distinguish initial discomfort from a clear mismatch. Trying something new can feel awkward before you understand it. ____4____ Ask whether another attempt might help, rather than treating the first nervous moment as a final judgment.

Finally, leave yourself time outside organised activities. ____5____ A choice can be worthwhile without filling every available afternoon. Joining fewer clubs may allow you to take part more fully in the ones you choose.

B. Choosing a club and taking a journey

Our class left for a museum visit on the ____1____ (twenty) of May. The teacher had reminded us to bring only a small bag, but I arrived with enough things for a whole weekend. A friend laughed and offered to help me carry it.

At the station, part of the entrance ____2____ (repair), so we followed the temporary signs. A member of staff showed us the route ____3____ led to the platforms. The teacher checked the group before we went through the barrier.

I had packed three books, thinking I would read throughout the journey. In fact, the ____4____ (discuss) about the exhibition began almost as soon as we sat down. We compared the objects we hoped to see and the questions we wanted to ask.

After ____5____ (reach) the museum, we put our bags in the lockers. Mine was ____6____ (heavy) than anyone else's, although the visit lasted only a few hours. I was glad not to carry it around every room.

Our guide encouraged us ____7____ (choose) one object to describe in detail. I selected a small wooden box ____8____ its painted lid interested me. The activity helped us slow down rather than hurry past everything.

On the train home, I looked through my notes and smiled at ____9____ (I) unnecessary packing. Next time, I would bring fewer objects and leave more room ____10____ questions. The most useful thing I carried home fitted on two pages.

A. Preparing to speak and looking at bubbles

Preparing an oral presentation is not simply writing an essay and reading it aloud. A listener cannot move backwards through a paragraph as easily as a reader can. The structure has to support attention as the talk unfolds.

Begin by deciding what listeners should understand at the end. A list of everything you know is not yet a message. ____1____ Other details should help that idea rather than compete with it.

Give the audience a route through the talk. A brief opening can explain the question, the stages and the reason it matters. ____2____ These signals help listeners place a detail in the larger explanation.

Rehearse aloud, not only in your head. A sentence that looks elegant may be hard to say clearly. ____3____ If you repeatedly run out of breath in the same place, the wording may need to change.

Use visual material for a clear purpose. A slide packed with text may force the audience to choose between reading and listening. ____4____ Explain the part you want them to notice rather than assuming that its importance is obvious.

Finally, leave space for questions and a short conclusion. ____5____ The aim is to make the main point easier to carry away, not to hide it inside a hurried list of unfinished extras.

B. Preparing to speak and looking at bubbles

A soap bubble looks simple, but each one ____1____ (contain) air enclosed by a very thin liquid film. The soap helps the film last long enough for us to watch it, although an ordinary bubble still changes from moment to moment.

When a bubble floats freely without touching anything, surface tension tends to draw it into a round shape. This is connected with the attraction ____2____ the molecules in the liquid. A sphere can enclose a given volume with the least surface area, which helps explain the shape.

The film becomes ____3____ (thin) as liquid drains and evaporates. Eventually, it breaks. Two bubbles ____4____ meet can affect one another's shape, so not every part of a group looks like a separate perfect sphere.

Before ____5____ (blow) bubbles in a classroom demonstration, our teacher asked us to think about what we wanted to observe. We were not trying to produce the largest possible number. We wanted to compare individual bubbles with those that joined together.

The changing ____6____ (shape) were easier to see against a dark background. We watched ____7____ (careful) and avoided treating a quick photograph as a record of every stage.

The activity gave us ____8____ useful starting point, but not a complete ____9____ (explain) of liquids and forces. Afterwards, our teacher connected the observations with ideas that could be discussed more ____10____ (precise) than "bubbles are always round". The familiar sight had become a question worth examining.

A demanding project can make a pause feel like a failure of commitment. Yet continuing without attention may waste more effort than stopping briefly. The useful question is not whether serious people ever rest, but how a pause can support a return to the work.
